title: The Tannisho, part two
hookLine: read the later sections on faith and doubt
tomorrow: who sings his teachings from a cave, and why sing them at all?

lines: QUOTED FOR WHAT HE NEVER SAID.
cards: A beloved coach retires, and within a season the new staff are quoting him for things he never said. The fans who knew him wince. Yuien, the student who wrote down Shinran's sayings, felt that wince.
After his teacher's death, he heard people teaching in Shinran's name things Shinran never taught. So he wrote it down, and the book's title says why: the Tannisho, notes lamenting the differences.

teach.b: In the later sections, Yuien takes the mistaken teachings one at a time. Some said you can't be born in the Pure Land unless you study the scriptures; Yuien answers that the nembutsu needs no learning.

teach.h: NO BIGGER BUDDHA FOR BIGGER GIFTS.
teach.b: Some said the bigger your gifts to the temple, the bigger the Buddha you'd become; Yuien calls that baseless. Notice the pattern. Each mistake adds a condition: be learned enough, be generous enough, be sure enough.
Then, near the end, a story. In Honen's circle, Shinran once said his entrusting and his teacher's were one and the same. Others objected: how could his match the master's?
Honen settled it: my shinjin is given by Amida, and so is Shinran's, so they are one. And Yuien remembers Shinran saying that when he pondered the vow, it seemed made for him, Shinran, alone.
Entrusted, in this record, means nothing added.
No test to pass first, no amount of certainty to reach. Just the weight, set down.

how: In Shin Buddhist temples, the Tannisho is read and discussed, and the nembutsu is said as thanks; some teachers point to Yuien's corrections when explaining that the teaching adds no conditions.

o: a list of the rules for monks in Japanese Pure Land temples
Shinran's sayings, kept by a student who feared distortion
a biography of Honen written by his chief disciple

games.q: the week's lines — tap the pairs.

s: Yuien wrote the Tannisho because people were teaching things Shinran never said
the title itself means notes lamenting the differences.
in the Tannisho, bigger gifts to the temple make a bigger Buddha
Yuien lists that as a mistake and rejects it.
in the epilogue story, Honen says Shinran's shinjin could never equal his own
Honen says both are given by Amida, so they are one.

games.q: your aunt hears a speaker say you have to study for years before your prayers 'count.' what would Yuien's corrections point to?
o: an added condition: his record says the nembutsu needs no learning.
a fair rule: real devotion has to be earned through study first.
a sign she should give more to the temple to make up for it.
games.why: Yuien's later sections push back on each added condition: learning, bigger gifts, more certainty. entrusting adds nothing.

practice: Write one worry on a scrap of paper, in a few plain words. Fold it once and set it down somewhere out of reach, a shelf, a drawer, under a cup. For the rest of the sit, let your hands rest empty in your lap, until the bell.

wordCard.voice: The Tannisho, part two: Yuien's corrections, and the story of the shinjin that Honen and Shinran shared. Entrusting, with nothing added.

orig.note: Japanese: notes (抄) lamenting (歎) differences (異), the title Yuien gave his record.

carryVoice: The line to take with you: entrusted, the worry still real and no longer carried alone. Eight of eleven, read.
